extracted.intended_audience: students, reformers, and legislators interested in constitutional design and the theory of representative government
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for structuring representative government (remuneration, term length, mandate/pledges, bicameralism, and selection of representatives), aimed at assessing institutional choices and electoral/legislative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration of members of Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: No remuneration which any one would think of attaching to the post would attract to it those who were seriously engaged in other lucrative professions; payment should be an indemnity for loss of time or money, not a salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A salary would make the occupation 'an object of desire to adventurers of a low class' and turn the seat into a pecuniary pursuit, producing demoralization and pandering to voters. Public subscription to support an entirely impecunious but pre-eminent person (e.g. 'like Andrew Marvel') is unobjectionable: it will only be given for striking personal qualities and tends to secure independence of opinion. Anti-pattern: turning the office into a paid profession that attracts those seeking pecuniary returns and encourages corruption (illustrated by the 'auction between Cleon and the sausage-seller').

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of parliamentary term — balance of accountability and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Members should not have so long a tenure that they forget responsibility or neglect constituent conferences, nor so short that they cannot be judged by a course of action rather than a single act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where democratic power is weak or representatives are immediately absorbed into courtly/aristocratic influences, frequent elections (even three years being almost too long) are necessary. Where democracy is ascendant and publicity/press are active, terms under five years may be insufficient to avoid timid subserviency. Seven years is 'unnecessary' but kept tolerable because of the possibility of earlier dissolution. Consider practical effects (e.g. last year of term mimics annual parliaments) when choosing term length.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of renewal — general vs gradual/partial renewal
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer general renewal of the whole House at term expiration rather than individual members vacating at different times (i.e., avoid gradual/partial renewal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: general renewal allows prompt removal of a majority offensive to the nation and provides a periodical general muster to gauge the national mind and relative party strength. Partial renewal risks long divergence between assembly and constituency by allowing a majority to retain many years of their term while new members are added 'drop by drop.' Even where partial renewal removes a large fraction (a third or a fifth), it does not conclusively ascertain national sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive power of dissolution (practical restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibility of earlier dissolution by the executive keeps motives for standing well with constituents always before the member's eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although detailed reasons are deferred to the chapter on the executive, the presence of dissolution power functions as a practical check on representatives' behavior and can justify longer nominal terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether electors may require pledges (delegate vs trustee/delegate question)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual pledges should not be required unless electors are so narrowed in choice by social circumstances that they must ensure a representative's fidelity to certain opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The delegation theory (representative as mere mouthpiece) is judged false and practically hurtful when constitutional safeguards for minority representation or vote differentiation do exist. Electors are entitled to full knowledge of candidate opinions and may properly reject candidates who differ on fundamental articles of belief. But, generally, representatives should have unfettered discretion to act according to their judgment; requiring absolute conformity to electors' opinions is unwise because superior ability may lead to different (often better) judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative independence and transparency of views
rubrics_metrics.description: A man of conscience and known ability should insist on full freedom to act as he deems best, but electors are entitled to know how he means to act — what opinions will guide his conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should disclose their political opinions on matters of public duty. Electors may overlook non-fundamental differences in favor of superior ability, but some convictions (those 'like his life-blood') are non-compromisable and justify dismissal if the representative acts against them. If a representative changes opinion honestly and openly, electors ought not to treat that as peremptory grounds for withdrawing confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When pledges are justified (narrowing of electoral choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pledges may be justified when electors, by social or institutional constraints, are compelled to choose representatives from persons of widely different class interests and have no reasonable alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such circumstances the electors may need to exact conditions to guard against representation hostile to their interests. Even then, they should prefer to seek representatives of superior ability and reserve pledges only as a necessary precaution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria/tests for electors to identify superior representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical signs by which ordinary electors can recognize men of superior political ability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary indicators: actual public services (having filled posts of magnitude and produced good results); authorship of measures shown by their effects to be wisely planned; successful predictions; advice whose adoption led to good consequences; reputation among disinterested persons conversant with the subject; recommendations by persons already looked up to. For untried persons, reputation for ability and endorsements are the best available tests. Electors should corroborate signs and consult general opinion of competent observers rather than rely on showy talent alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of constitutional morality (temper of actors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond written law, doctrines of constitutional morality — maxims of conduct and forbearance — are essential to the beneficial operation of representative government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These unwritten maxims restrain excesses in imbalanced governments and preserve checks and limitations where positive institutional guarantees are imperfect. Institutional design should assume and cultivate these moral maxims because they materially affect how powers are actually used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of votes to authenticated education (cultivating deference to ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions should stamp opinions of persons of a more educated class as entitled to greater weight; assigning plurality of votes to authenticated superiority of education would give tone to public feeling in favor of deference to mental superiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is defended not solely for direct political consequences but for its cultural effect in promoting reverence for superior intellect; it is proposed as a way to counteract democratic tendencies that undervalue personal superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and value of a Second Chamber (bicameralism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two Chambers may be useful chiefly to prevent the corrupting influence of undivided power and to inculcate conciliation and mutual give-and-take; if all other constitutional questions are rightly decided, whether one or two chambers exist is of comparatively little importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both chambers are similarly composed, the necessity of consent of both may delay measures but can prompt appeals to the nation and prevent precipitancy; if they are dissimilarly composed (an aristocratic check on democracy), their efficacy depends on the social support and external power base of the second chamber — an aristocratic upper house is ineffective in a truly democratic society. The chief practical advantage of bicameralism is psychological and institutional: preventing any set of persons from acting as if they were the only authority and promoting compromise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of bicameral houses — similar vs dissimilar composition
rubrics_metrics.description: If two chambers are of similar composition, both will obey the same influences; if dissimilar, the second chamber's capacity to check the other depends on its external social basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar composition: less likelihood of radically different outcomes; may cause delay but also enable appeal to the electorate. Dissimilar composition: an aristocratic chamber can only act as an effective check where the social order supports it; otherwise it will be ineffectual against democratic forces.
